summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has never been criminalised in Cambodia; the country inherited no sodomy statute under the French protectorate and none was enacted after independence in 1953. The age of consent is 15 and applies regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans visitors have no route to legal recognition. Cambodian law does not permit changes to gender markers on official documents, and gender-affirming surgery is not legally available. The statutory framework contains no non-discrimination provisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

The state's formal posture is cooperative. At the 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cambodia accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage; at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 recommendations on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, covering marriage equality, legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures. The inventory contains no evidence that implementing legislation has been enacted. Cambodia also hosted the visit of the UN Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose report identified good practices, remaining challenges and recommendations to strengthen protection; an unofficial Khmer translation was produced for national stakeholders.

Lived conditions diverge sharply from that posture. A Cambodian Centre for Human Rights study documented harassment and abuse against more than 135 transgender women on the country's city streets, describing the level of abuse as shocking. It recorded a practice in Siem Reap in which police targeted transgender sex workers and forced them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water, sometimes naked, and to leave the area; cisgender sex workers were not documented as receiving the same treatment. The same 2016 study found about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested, with more than 90% of them stating the arrest was because they were transgender.

Family rejection is a principal exposure. A Rainbow Community Kampuchea study reported in 2019 found 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 had suffered emotional abuse by a family member, and 35% of participants under 35 had considered suicide because of family rejection, including a 27-year-old trans man forced by his mother into rehabilitation to 'fix his gender'.

Prison placement is decided administratively rather than by statute. In February 2025 the president of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee stated at a public handover ceremony that transgender offenders who had undergone sex-change surgery were transferred from Correctional Centre 1, the men's facility, to Correctional Centre 2, the women's facility at Prey Sar prison in Phnom Penh. The statement was made in praise of the centre and cites no published regulation or policy text.

Public visibility is real but concentrated. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have a visible LGBT bar and club scene, and Pride parades have run annually since 2003, with the first Siem Reap Pride in 2018. In 2017 the US State Department listed violence against LGBTI persons among Cambodia's most significant human rights issues, noting frequent harassment over appearance and work in entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organisation, while finding no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care.
tangentialFactors:
A pattern of official welcome messaging exists alongside the enforcement record. In February 2011 Cambodian tourism businesses launched the 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign to signal welcome to LGBT tourists, and the Ministry of Tourism endorsed it, stating it had no policy to discriminate and supported the sector. In 2015 the Ministry of Information wrote to media outlets asking them to stop mocking the LGBT community, citing constitutional protection of LGBT honour and rights.

Statements by officials on the reach of existing law have been contested domestically. In 2015 a Council of Ministers spokesman claimed that existing law already protected LGBT people; the Cambodian Center for Human Rights disputed the claim. The 2017 State Department reporting also noted increased government restrictions on speech, assembly and press freedom in the country generally.

Official hostility at the highest level has been recorded: in 2007 Prime Minister Hun Sen publicly disowned and disinherited his adopted daughter because she is a lesbian.
localsOnly:
Education policy was reworked toward LGBT inclusion. In June 2017 the government announced new life-skills courses covering sexual health, gender-based violence, gender identity and combating discrimination against the LGBT population; these became part of the curriculum in all Cambodian schools in 2018. Before the rollout, LGBT activists working with the Ministry of Education trained more than 3,000 teachers in 20 schools across nine provinces. Many LGBT Cambodians nonetheless report bullying at school, and in January 2019 Cambodia received UN recommendations from Iceland, Mexico, Sweden and Uruguay to establish educational programmes and awareness campaigns on LGBT people and discrimination.

In 2019 the director of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee reported rising HIV infections within the LGBT community, particularly among people under 30. A 2010 report described a concentration of poor and working-class LGBT people in Beoung Kak 2, which was dubbed Cambodia's first gay town. Prison overcrowding has worsened because of arrests following a gang crackdown.
outOfScopeNotes:
The relationship between the accepted 2024 Universal Periodic Review recommendations and domestic legislation is unresolved in the inventory. Acceptance is recorded as a stated commitment; no source in the inventory confirms that implementing statutes on marriage equality, legal gender recognition or non-discrimination have been enacted, and the record states only the current absence of such provisions.

The February 2025 account of transferring post-surgical transgender prisoners between Correctional Centre 1 and Correctional Centre 2 rests on an official's remarks at an event. No statute, sub-decree or published regulation establishing this practice is cited, and it is unresolved whether the arrangement is written policy, an informal practice, or case-by-case.

A 2014 UNDP and USAID review of the legal and social environment for LGBT people in Cambodia, and a Frommer's travel guide section offering practical advice for gay and lesbian travellers, are in the inventory but were not relied on for specific legal or safety findings beyond their general scope.
